metadata.title: The Real Engine Behind Apple Stock's Next Potential Climb

content.text:
The company just posted a record-breaking quarter, but the most compelling part of its story might be the sales it couldn't even make.
After a run of more than fifty percent in the last year, you might be wondering what could possibly be left in the tank for Apple (AAPL). The company just posted a record-breaking quarter with revenue of $111.2 billion, up 17% from a year ago. That kind of performance, at this scale, is stunning.
But the most intriguing clue about Apple's future might not be in the numbers it printed, but in the constant caveat attached to them: "despite supply constraints."
A Product Cycle For The History Books
The engine here is the iPhone. In the most recent quarter, iPhone revenue grew 22% year-over-year to a record $57 billion. Management described customer enthusiasm as "extraordinary" and called the iPhone 17 family the "most popular lineup in our history when looking at the launch through the March quarter."
This isn't just a strong upgrade cycle. It's a demand signal so powerful that it's pushing Apple's twelve-month revenue growth to 12.8%, well ahead of its 5.6% three-year average. The business is running hot.
Demand Is Outpacing Supply
Here's where it gets interesting. That 22% iPhone growth came while the company was supply-constrained. The story continues into the next quarter. Management's forecast for the June quarter total company revenue to grow by 14% to 17% year-over-year explicitly "comprehends our best view of constraint supply."
Think about that. The official guidance, which points to continued double-digit growth, already assumes Apple won't be able to build every device it could otherwise sell. This suggests a deep well of underlying demand that the reported financials may not fully reflect. If Apple can solve its supply issues, there's a powerful, organic growth driver waiting to be unlocked.
The Price Of Performance
Of course, there's a catch. The very components that make these devices possible are getting more expensive. The company expects "significantly higher memory costs" in the June quarter. More pointedly, an executive warned that beyond June, "we believe memory costs will drive an increasing impact on our business."
This looming margin pressure runs directly against the force of this historic iPhone demand. With the company's operating margin already at a three-year peak of 32.6%, there isn't much room for error. Keep your eyes on the next gross margin forecast; it will be the first sign of whether rising costs can slow this sales momentum.
